# Instructor Guide — Part 1 (12/4, Hour 1): Choosing and Building the Right Forecast {#sec-mod5-part1-guide}

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How to use this guide"}
This is a facilitation guide for the instructor, not student-facing reading. It pairs with the slide deck `mod5_part1_slides.qmd`. Students arrive having read the full forecasting toolkit: time-series structure, trend, seasonality, and naive forecasts (@sec-week12-01), moving averages and exponential smoothing (@sec-week12-02), and regression-based forecasting, accuracy, and scenario analysis (@sec-week12-03), the last of which already introduced the Ceres Gardening Company case students will work with in Parts 2 and 3. This hour is a fast, live-coding synthesis of the whole toolkit before the afternoon applies it to Ceres.
:::

## Session Objectives

By the end of this period, students should be able to:

1. Recall and choose among the forecasting toolkit (naive, seasonal naive, moving average, exponential smoothing, Holt-Winters, regression-based) given a described business series.
2. Reconstruct a forecast, its accuracy comparison, and its interval, live, tying together all three reading sections.
3. Explain, in one sentence, why Ceres's own annual reporting isn't enough on its own for some of this toolkit.

## Detailed Run of Show

### Welcome and Reconnecting to Module 4's Close (10 min)

Recall the closing slide of Module 4 (@sec-mod4-part3-guide): "Module 4 added **build a model** to the decision cycle. Next: **forecasting**, predicting a value forward in **time**." Restate plainly: every method this morning still fits the same "build a model" step, but now the whole point is that order matters, we're predicting a series' own future from its own past (and, in the regression case, from calendar time itself).

### Live Coding: The Full Toolkit, Back to Back (20 min)

Rebuild the coffee shop example live, quickly, treating it as a recall exercise rather than new teaching:

1. `as_tsibble()` and `autoplot()` (@sec-week12-01).
2. `NAIVE()` and `SNAIVE()`, noting the seasonal naive forecast's tighter interval (@sec-week12-01).
3. A 7-day moving average, and why it blurs away which day of the week is being forecast (@sec-week12-02).
4. `ETS()` fit as Holt-Winters, comparing AICc against simpler exponential smoothing versions (@sec-week12-02).
5. `TSLM(revenue ~ trend() + dow)`, noting the `new_data()` requirement for its external `dow` predictor (@sec-week12-03).
6. The train/test accuracy table, all four methods landing close together once seasonality is modeled at all (@sec-week12-03).

Move briskly, students have already read every step of this; the goal is fluency, not first exposure.

### Activity: Which Method Would You Use? (25 min)

Hand out (or project) six short scenarios. In groups, identify which forecasting tool fits best, no calculation, a diagnosis exercise exactly like @sec-mod3-part1-guide's "which test would you use?" activity.

::: {.example title="Scenarios for the activity"}
1. A retailer's daily sales show no clear trend or repeating pattern, just noise around a stable average. *(Simple exponential smoothing)*
2. A call center's hourly call volume has a strong, stable day-of-week pattern and no real long-term trend. *(Seasonal naive, or Holt-Winters with no trend)*
3. A subscription company's monthly revenue has both a clear upward trend and a consistent end-of-quarter spike. *(Holt-Winters, or a regression with trend and a quarter-end indicator)*
4. A manager needs a same-day sales estimate and has no time to fit anything, just wants a quick, sensible baseline. *(Naive or seasonal naive, whichever fits the data's seasonality)*
5. An analyst wants to know exactly how many dollars a specific calendar day (say, every Friday) differs from a Monday, in a model that also accounts for a rising trend. *(Regression-based forecasting, TSLM with trend and day-of-week dummies)*
6. A planner wants to smooth out a noisy daily series to see the underlying trend, without needing to forecast anything yet. *(A moving average, used descriptively rather than as a forecast)*
:::

Circulate and listen for the most common error: reaching for Holt-Winters or a regression by default even when a series shows no real trend or seasonality (scenario 1), where the simplest tool is actually correct. Reinforce @sec-week12-01's point directly: complexity has to earn its keep.

### Debrief and Bridge to Ceres (5 min)

Debrief scenario 3 explicitly, then bridge: "This afternoon, we apply exactly this kind of judgment to a real company. Ceres Gardening Company's CEO has two things on his to-do list: a motivational speech for his sales team, and a meeting with the bank about growth and cash flow for next year. We're going to help with the second one." Note that Ceres's own financial reporting is **annual only**, five or six data points, nowhere near enough for moving averages or seasonality detection, which is exactly why Part 2 will bring in a supplementary monthly series to practice those tools at a realistic business cadence before returning to Ceres's own numbers.
